ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In Diagram A, the large circle represents the twilight circle; point P is located at the very top of the circle and is tangent to the dashed small circle representing the Arctic Circle; point Q is in the middle-lower part of Diagram A, and the question stem states that Q is (0°,90°E), with local time 12 o’clock. Diagram B is a graph of solar altitude changing with time; the horizontal axis marks 0, 12, and 24 o’clock, and the vertical axis marks 0° and 50°; among them there are multiple numbered curves, and curve ③ shows that the solar altitude is 0° at 0 o’clock and 24 o’clock, and reaches a maximum value close to 50° around 12 o’clock. Then reason: P is the tangent point between the Arctic Circle and the twilight circle, and the local time at point Q is 12 o’clock, so it can be judged that on this day the Arctic Circle is in the critical state of polar day, and at point P the midnight sun is just on the horizon. Take the latitude of P as φ=66.5°N, and the solar direct latitude as δ=23.5°N, then the noon solar altitude at P is about 90°-66.5°+23.5°=47°, approximately 50° in the diagram; the midnight solar altitude is 66.5°+23.5°-90°=0°. Therefore, the solar altitude at P on that day should be 0° at 0 o’clock and 24 o’clock, and reach about 50° at 12 o’clock, corresponding to curve ③ in Diagram B.

Then reason: P is the tangent point between the Arctic Circle and the twilight circle, and the local time at point Q is 12 o’clock, so it can be judged that on this day the Arctic Circle is in the critical state of polar day, and at point P the midnight sun is just on the horizon. Take the latitude of P as φ=66.5°N, and the solar direct latitude as δ=23.5°N, then the noon solar altitude at P is about 90°-66.5°+23.5°=47°, approximately 50° in the diagram; the midnight solar altitude is 66.5°+23.5°-90°=0°. Therefore, the solar altitude at P on that day should be 0° at 0 o’clock and 24 o’clock, and reach about 50° at 12 o’clock, corresponding to curve ③ in Diagram B.
